newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO should be ready to expand in 1999 - official.
newsitem.headline: NATO should be ready to expand in 1999 - official.

text.p: NATO should be ready to start taking in new members from central Europe in two years, Senator William Roth, the new head of the North Atlantic Assembly (NAA), the alliance's parliamentary arm, said on Tuesday.

"I am hopeful that in the 50th year of the alliance, that will be in two years from now in 1999, the first countries to be included will become members," Roth, a Republican from Delaware, told reporters on a brief visit to NATO headquarters.
Roth, who recently took over the post from Germany's Karsten Voigt, was on a fact-finding tour of the capitals of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's 16 members.
"We are trying to produce stability and security in central and eastern Europe. Our policy is inclusion not exclusion. Cooperation not confrontation," Roth said.

NATO has been drawing up a list of the state of readiness of the east and central European nations who are potential members. A summit of the alliance's leaders, likely to take place in the middle of next year, is due to select those for the first wave.

"It is clear that all 11 potential new member nations are not going to be admitted at one time...so it is important that we make clear by actions and words that it is a continuing process," Roth said.
"Hungary, Poland, Romania, the Czech Republic and Slovenia have all been identified as potential members.
"What we are really seeking in central Europe is to fill a vacuum. It is in everyone's interests. We assure by providing stability and security that the reforms will continue," he said.
Roth said the chief obstacle to NATO taking in former foes along its eastern flank was Russia's attitude, which wavers between outright condemnation and muted resistance.
"We are seeking a special relationship of cooperation with Russia. A democratic Russia has nothing to fear," he said.

Roth said that despite evidence the United States was becoming more concerned with domestic than foreign issues, and the standoff between Washington and Paris over command of NATO's southern forces, support for the alliance remained solid.
"A recent poll showed that 75 percent of American people approved of NATO," he said.
"It is an alliance that was successful. It brought about peace without war. What we are seeking is to modify the alliance to make it ready for the 21st century."
NATO is in the throes of redesigning its decision-making and command structures to both give it a more European flavour, to cut costs and reaction times and prepare for eastward expansion.

But France, which less than a year ago came almost all the way back in from the cold by rejoining many of NATO structures it turned its back on in the 1960s, has thrown a spanner in the works by insisting that a European runs the southern command.
The United States has always held the military reins of power in NATO and is not about to give up any of it.
"I support the United States' position. It is an area where we have deep involvement," Roth said. "But I don't think the issue will have any significant impact on (U.S.) attitudes to NATO."
